title: A new hepatitis B drug is 20 genetic letters that pair with the virus's RNA
body: On 20 October 2026, the US Food and Drug Administration approved bepirovirsen, sold as Hibsago, for some adults with chronic hepatitis B, [GSK announced](https://www.gsk.com/media/alvmln3q/final-2-_bepi_us_approval_sea_201026.pdf). It is an antisense drug: a chain of 20 genetic letters that pairs with a stretch of the virus's RNA messages, a stretch that its [US label](https://gskpro.com/content/dam/global/hcpportal/en_US/Prescribing_Information/Hibsago/pdf/HIBSAGO-PI-MG-IFU.PDF) says is identical in 97.6% of 9,139 hepatitis B genomes. The cell's own enzyme RNase H1 cuts RNA paired with DNA like this, so infected liver cells make less of the virus's DNA and proteins, including its surface protein. Standard pills block the enzyme that copies the virus, but not these messages. In two trials, after 24 weeks of injections on top of their pills, 19% of patients (233 of 1,220) had no detectable virus DNA or surface protein 24 weeks after stopping all treatment, a 'functional cure', against none of 614 on placebo.

slides.question: Out of 10 people given the new hepatitis B drug in trials, how many had no detectable virus 24 weeks after stopping?
slides.explanation: About 2 in 10: 233 of 1,220 (19%) had no detectable virus DNA or surface protein 24 weeks after stopping all treatment, a functional cure. On placebo: 0 of 614.

slides.alt: Animation in plum and mint: a liver cell's nucleus holds viral DNA that keeps sending out RNA messages and surface protein. Letters pair, A with U and G with C; the 20-letter drug zips onto its RNA target and the enzyme RNase H1 cuts it. Then 9,139 genomes, 24 weeks of injections, 19% against 0%.

slides.prompt: Slide the 20 letters of the hepatitis B drug bepirovirsen along a stretch of the virus's RNA. Where do all 20 pair up?
slides.takeaway: Only at its target, which the drug's label says is identical in 97.6% of 9,139 hepatitis B genomes. Anywhere else, at most 11 letters pair by chance.

slides.heading: How the antisense drug bepirovirsen works

steps.label: A strand of 20 genetic letters is injected
It pairs with the virus's RNA in liver cells
The cell's enzyme RNase H1 cuts that RNA
Less virus DNA and surface protein are made

slides.heading: Two ways to fight hepatitis B

left.label: Standard pills
left.text: Block the enzyme that copies the virus's genes into new DNA. Usually taken for years: under 1% reach a functional cure in a year, says drugmaker GSK.

right.label: Bepirovirsen
right.text: Pairs with the virus's RNA messages so they are cut. Weekly injections for 24 weeks, added to the pills: 19% reached a functional cure in trials.

slides.heading: Who it is approved for
slides.text: In the US, bepirovirsen is approved for adults without cirrhosis whose virus DNA is already kept down by at least 6 months of standard pills, and whose surface protein is at most 3,000 units per millilitre. Its label warns of liver flares and drops in blood platelets, so patients are tested often.

slides.question: What does the new hepatitis B drug bepirovirsen pair with?
slides.explanation: Its 20 letters pair with a stretch of the virus's RNA. The cell's enzyme RNase H1 then cuts that RNA, so the cell makes less virus DNA and protein.
